questions.stem: Exact data give $p(0)=1$, $p(1)=2$, $p(2)=5$ and $p(3)=10$. First assume $p$ is a real polynomial of degree at most three: determine it and justify uniqueness. Then remove the degree bound and characterise every real polynomial consistent with the same four data points. State precisely which inference depended on the bound.

answer.summary: For degree at most 3, p(x)=x^2+1; uniqueness follows because the difference of two such polynomials has four distinct zeros but degree at most 3. Without the bound, p=x^2+1+x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)q for arbitrary real polynomial q. The degree bound is exactly what forces q=0.
reasoning: Separate what the bounded and unbounded parts are asking. Two inference problems with different admissible classes.
Compare p with x^2+1 and form their difference. A difference polynomial with four named roots.
Use the degree bound to decide whether that difference can be nonzero. The bounded candidate is forced and unique.
Remove the degree bound by factoring every difference that vanishes at all four nodes. The complete unrestricted family and the exact inference that used the bound.

questions.stem: A nonzero real polynomial has degree at most four and zeros at $-2$, $0$ and $2$. It changes sign across each of $-2$ and $2$, but has the same nonzero sign on the two sides sufficiently close to $0$. Also $p(1)=-3$. Construct the polynomial, justify the multiplicity information you use, and establish whether these conditions determine it uniquely. These are exact benchmark conditions, not measurements from a graph.

questions.stem: Find the least possible degree of a real polynomial whose distinct real zeros are exactly $-1$ and $1$, and which satisfies $p(0)=p(2)=1$. Exhibit one such polynomial, verify that it has no other real zeros, and prove that every smaller degree is impossible. You may use continuity of real polynomial functions and the factor theorem. This is an advanced competition extension.

answer.summary: Write p=(x^2-1)g, so g(0)=-1 and g(2)=1/3. Degree 2 is impossible; degree 3 forces a linear g with extra zero 3/2; degree 4 forces a quadratic g that changes sign on (0,2), hence has a real zero there and cannot avoid an extra distinct zero. Degree 5 works: p=(1/3)(x+1)(x-1)^2(x^2-3x+3); the quadratic discriminant is -3.
reasoning: Factor out the two required real zeros and translate the two value conditions to the remaining factor. Constraints g(0)=-1 and g(2)=1/3.
Eliminate total degrees 2 and 3. Degrees 2 and 3 are impossible.
Eliminate total degree 4 using the sign change of g between 0 and 2. Degree 4 is impossible without an extra distinct real zero.
Construct a degree-5 example with a repeated allowed root and a quadratic having no real roots. A verified degree-5 witness, proving minimality.

reasoning_route.action: Factor out the two required real zeros and translate the two value conditions to the remaining factor.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The factor theorem gives p=(x^2-1)g and the values determine g(0),g(2).
reasoning_route.output: Constraints g(0)=-1 and g(2)=1/3.

reasoning_route.action: Eliminate total degrees 2 and 3.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A constant g cannot take both required values; a linear g is forced and its real zero creates an extra zero of p.
reasoning_route.output: Degrees 2 and 3 are impossible.

reasoning_route.action: Eliminate total degree 4 using the sign change of g between 0 and 2.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Continuity forces a real zero of the quadratic g in (0,2); a quadratic cannot have only a sign-changing double root at 1, and a simple root at 1 forces another real root.
reasoning_route.output: Degree 4 is impossible without an extra distinct real zero.

reasoning_route.action: Construct a degree-5 example with a repeated allowed root and a quadratic having no real roots.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A negative quadratic discriminant prevents extra real zeros while the value constraints can be met exactly.
reasoning_route.output: A verified degree-5 witness, proving minimality.

questions.stem: An open box is formed by cutting squares of side $x$ cm from the corners of a $10$ cm square sheet and folding the sides up, ignoring thickness. An exact calculation table gives volumes $0$, $64$ and $72$ cubic centimetres at $x=0,1,2$ respectively; $x=0$ denotes the flat limiting configuration. An analyst fits $Q(x)=-28x^2+92x$ to these three entries and treats it as the volume model. Derive the model from the geometry, state the domain for a non-degenerate box, assess the fitted model over that domain, and choose an additional admissible input that discriminates between the two accounts. Explain why matching the recorded entries is insufficient.

answer.summary: Geometry gives V=x(10-2x)^2 on 0<x<5. The fitted Q=-28x^2+92x matches the three recorded rows but Q-V=-4x(x-1)(x-2). At admissible x=4, V=16 while Q=-80. Finite agreement is not a geometric model or an unrestricted identity proof.
reasoning: Derive the box volume from its dimensions after the cuts. V=x(10-2x)^2 with the physical dimensions visible.
State the non-degenerate domain and decide which account is a model versus an interpolant. A physical model/domain and a separate empirical interpolant.
Compare the two formulas algebraically and choose a new admissible input. A discriminating exact calculation.
Check that the new input lies in the physical domain and that volume remains nonnegative. A domain-consistent rejection of the fitted quadratic as the volume model.

reasoning_route.action: Derive the box volume from its dimensions after the cuts.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Base-area times height is the governing geometry, not an arbitrary curve fit.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Positive height and base side constrain x; matching three rows alone does not encode the construction.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Their difference exposes the recorded interpolation nodes; a new point tests whether the accounts agree away from them.
reasoning_route.output: A discriminating exact calculation.

reasoning_route.why_valid: A geometric volume cannot become negative on a valid box domain.
reasoning_route.output: A domain-consistent rejection of the fitted quadratic as the volume model.

questions.stem: For real $a$, let $R_a(x)=[x^2-(a+1)x+a]/(x-a)$ with its original domain $x\neq a$. A student cancels a factor and says that every $R_a$ is the same polynomial function on all real numbers, with zero $1$. Determine which parts of that statement hold on the original domains, classify the real zeros as $a$ varies, and describe the polynomial extension separately. Explain why extending a function and preserving its original domain are different operations.

answer.summary: The numerator is (x-a)(x-1), so R_a=x-1 only on x!=a. If a!=1, x=1 is an allowed zero; if a=1 it is excluded and there are no zeros. The polynomial extension x-1 is defined on all reals and always has zero 1; filling the hole changes the function domain.
reasoning: Factor the numerator and cancel only under the original restriction x!=a. The simplified rule x-1 on R\{a}.
Classify whether x=1 is an allowed zero as a varies. One zero when a!=1; no zeros when a=1.
Describe the polynomial extension separately from the original function. The all-real polynomial x-1, distinguished from every R_a.

reasoning_route.action: Factor the numerator and cancel only under the original restriction x!=a.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Division by x-a is valid only where that factor is nonzero.
reasoning_route.output: The simplified rule x-1 on R\{a}.

reasoning_route.action: Classify whether x=1 is an allowed zero as a varies.
reasoning_route.why_valid: A zero must both make the rule zero and belong to the function's domain.
reasoning_route.output: One zero when a!=1; no zeros when a=1.

reasoning_route.action: Describe the polynomial extension separately from the original function.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Extension intentionally assigns a value at the hole; simplification alone does not alter the original domain.
reasoning_route.output: The all-real polynomial x-1, distinguished from every R_a.

questions.stem: A real polynomial $p$ has degree at most four, satisfies $p(-x)=p(x)$ for every real $x$, and has $p(1)=p(2)=0$ and $p(0)=4$. Classify the following claims as necessary, possible but not necessary, or impossible under these conditions: its degree is two; it has exactly four distinct real zeros; it also has zero $3$; its leading coefficient is $1$; the data determine a unique polynomial. Justify each verdict. Reassess the claims when the degree bound is removed, while all other conditions are retained.

answer.summary: With degree at most 4, evenness forces roots ±1,±2 and p(0)=4 gives p=(x^2-1)(x^2-4). Thus degree2 impossible, exactly four distinct real zeros necessary, zero3 impossible, leading coefficient1 necessary, and uniqueness necessary. Without the degree bound, p=(x^2-1)(x^2-4)h with even h and h(0)=1; only degree2 remains impossible, while the other bounded conclusions become possible-but-not-necessary or uniqueness becomes false.
reasoning: Use evenness to reflect the given positive zeros and factor the four forced roots. Forced factors (x^2-1)(x^2-4).
Use degree at most 4 and p(0)=4 to close the bounded case. One bounded polynomial.
Classify every claim from that bounded polynomial. Five bounded verdicts.
Remove the degree bound by parameterizing every even multiplier that preserves p(0)=4. Complete unbounded family and revised claim statuses.

questions.stem: Real polynomials $p$ and $q$ each have degree at most three. They agree at $x=-1,0,1$, but $p(2)-q(2)=12$. Characterise every possible difference polynomial, determine $p(3)-q(3)$, and decide whether the evidence identifies either polynomial individually. Use explicit examples to separate uniqueness of a difference from uniqueness of its two components.

answer.summary: d=p-q has degree at most 3 and roots -1,0,1, so d=kx(x^2-1). d(2)=12 gives k=2 and d(3)=48. p and q are not individually identified: choose any cubic-or-less r and set q=r, p=r+d.

Use d(2)=12 to determine k, then evaluate d(3). The unique difference polynomial and d(3).

questions.stem: Characterise all monic real polynomials of degree at most four whose distinct real zeros are exactly $-1$ and $1$ and whose value at zero is $1$. Explain how repeated factors and any remaining quadratic factor affect completeness of your list. Prove both that every item in your list works and that no allowed polynomial has been omitted.

answer.summary: Let multiplicities at 1 and -1 be m,n>=1. With no leftover factor, p(0)=(-1)^m=1, so m is even; degree at most 4 gives (m,n)=(2,1) or (2,2). A leftover monic quadratic can only occur with m=n=1; p(0)=1 then forces constant -1, giving discriminant b^2+4>0 and unwanted real roots. Hence exactly (x-1)^2(x+1) and (x-1)^2(x+1)^2.
reasoning: Write the required factors with positive multiplicities and isolate any remaining monic factor. A finite multiplicity/remainder case structure.
Enumerate multiplicity choices allowed by degree and p(0)=1 when no remainder remains. Two direct candidate multiplicity patterns.
Eliminate the only possible quadratic remainder case. Any such remainder creates forbidden real zeros.
Check monicity, degree, p(0) and exact distinct real zero set for each surviving polynomial. A complete two-polynomial classification.

questions.stem: A solver uses four rules: cancellation makes a rational expression a polynomial on all real numbers; the largest printed exponent is always the degree; a degree-$n$ polynomial has exactly $n$ distinct real zeros; agreement at three inputs proves an identity. Develop a qualified decision procedure and apply it to: $A_t(x)=(t-1)x^3+x^2-1$ with real $t$; $B(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ on its original domain; $C(x)=(x-2)^2(x^2+1)$; and the pair $D(x)=x^2+1$, $E(x)=x^2+1+x(x-1)(x-2)$ compared at $x=0,1,2$. State the relevant conditions and valid conclusions in each case, then create one fresh counterexample to an unqualified rule. Preserve the difference between expressions, functions, identities and finite observations.

answer.summary: Cancellation preserves equality only on the original domain; degree is read after simplification and parameter leading-coefficient checks; a nonzero degree-n polynomial has at most n distinct real zeros; finite agreement proves identity only with a suitable degree bound on the difference. Fresh counterexample: (x-3)^2/(x-3) on x!=3.
